overview:
Abraham, now old, makes his chief servant swear to find Isaac a wife among his own kin in Mesopotamia and never to take Isaac back there. The servant travels with ten camels to the city of Nahor, stops at the well at evening, and asks God for a sign: the girl who offers water to him and to his camels. Rebekah does just that, and she turns out to be Abraham's great-niece. Her brother Laban welcomes the servant, who tells the whole story over again. The family agrees, Rebekah says “I will go,” and Isaac brings her into Sarah's tent.

At 67 verses this is the longest chapter in Genesis, and much of the length is repetition: the servant retells to Rebekah's family nearly everything the reader has just watched. The small changes in his version show a careful negotiator at work.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Genesis.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional chronology places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC. Isaac is 40 when he marries Rebekah (25:20), three years after Sarah's death.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Abraham's home in Canaan to “Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor” (v. 10), in the Haran region, then back to Isaac in the south country near the well Lahai-roi (v. 62).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: The servant's own retelling (vv. 34–49). Abraham 2:2–5 places Nahor, Milcah, and Terah's household in Haran.

hermeneutics:
Israel's storytellers had a stock scene for finding a wife, which Robert Alter calls the betrothal type-scene: a man travels to a foreign land and meets a young woman at a well, water is drawn, she runs home with the news, and a meal and a marriage follow. Jacob meets Rachel this way (29:1–14), and Moses meets Zipporah (Exodus 2:15–21). Hearers who knew the pattern would notice what is different here. The groom stays home and a servant stands in for him, and the woman is the one who draws the water, runs, and acts. That fits the Rebekah who later steers Jacob's blessing (ch. 27).

The “city of Nahor” (v. 10) may be a real place as well as a family name. Letters from Mari (18th century BC) and later Assyrian texts name a town called Nahur in the upper Euphrates region near Haran, and nearby towns carry names like Serug's (11:20–23). The servant's long trip north is a trip back to the family's home country, the land Abraham was called to leave.

Marriage in the ancient Near East was a contract between households. Old Babylonian law speaks of a betrothal payment (*terhatum*) brought by the groom's side to the bride's family, and the Laws of Hammurabi (§§159–161) settle what happens if either side backs out after gifts are given. The servant's gold for Rebekah and his “precious things” for her brother and mother (v. 53) fit that pattern. So does Laban's leading role with the mother: Bethuel, the father, speaks only once (v. 50).

notes: **Changes in the retelling:** in the event he gives the gifts before asking her family (vv. 22–23); telling it, he asks first (v. 47), so the family hears of a properly conducted approach. He leaves out Abraham's warning never to take Isaac back (vv. 6, 8) and opens with Abraham's wealth and Isaac as sole heir (vv. 35–36).

**The LORD at every step:** the divine name occurs 19 times in the Hebrew. Prayer (v. 12), praise (v. 27), and worship (vv. 26, 52) mark each stage, and the family's answer is “The thing proceedeth from the LORD” (v. 50).
**A nameless servant:** he is called “servant” 15 times in Hebrew but never named, while the people he serves and meets all are.

The search for Rebekah closes Abraham's active part in the story; his charge to the servant (vv. 2–8) is the last thing he says in Genesis. Isaac meets Rebekah coming from Lahai-roi (v. 62), the well where the angel found Hagar (16:14), and the unit ends with Abraham's death and Ishmael's line (25:1–18).

**Forward:** Jacob also finds his wife at a well in the same family's country (29:1–14). Rebekah's family blesses her that her seed may “possess the gate of those which hate them” (v. 60), close to God's oath to Abraham in 22:17.

traditions.text: Abraham's account says Nahor married Milcah, the daughter of Haran, and that Terah stayed behind in Haran and “turned again unto his idolatry.” That background explains both halves of Abraham's charge: the bride should come from his own kin, but Isaac must not go back to the land and household Abraham was called out of. Abraham 2:6 also records the promise of the land to his seed, which Abraham repeats to the servant in v. 7.

Reads Rebekah at the well as the model teacher. She goes down to the spring of God's wisdom and comes up filled; she carries a pitcher where Hagar carried a bulky skin; she lowers it onto her arm so the learner gets what he can take; and she gives more than the little he asked for. Watering the camels means training memory, since the camel chews its food over again.

Explains the oath under the thigh as both men placing a hand under each other's thigh and calling on God as witness. At the well the other girls refuse the stranger water, saying they need it all at home, and Rebekah rebukes them. She also tells him that her father Bethuel is dead, so Laban and her mother run the household, which would explain why Bethuel hardly appears.

Asks the same question about Bethuel and answers it differently: he tried to block the match and died that night, so the “few days” the family asks for in v. 55 are the week of mourning. From “we will inquire at her mouth” (v. 57) it draws the rule that an orphan girl may be married only with her consent. Josephus has Bethuel dead before the servant arrives; the midrash has him die during the visit.

Notices the chapter's length. The ordinary talk of the patriarchs' servants, it says, is dearer to God than the Torah of their descendants: the story of Abraham's servant fills two or three columns and is told twice, while some laws of purity are learned only from a single extra letter.

With the rabbis, Rashi takes the servant to be Eliezer of Damascus (15:2). In v. 39 the word for “peradventure” is spelled so that it can be read “to me,” and the midrash hears Eliezer hoping Abraham would turn to him and take his own daughter for Isaac. Abraham refuses: his son is blessed, he answers, and Eliezer is under a curse, and the two cannot be joined.

Collects midrashic details the text leaves out. The servant ran to Rebekah because he saw the water rise in the well to meet her; he came “this day” (v. 42) because the road shrank for him and he arrived the day he set out. Isaac was coming from Lahai-roi (v. 62) because he had gone to bring Hagar back to Abraham as a wife, a reading that sets up Rashi's view of Keturah in ch. 25.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 24:17, 42, 62 (from Genesis Rabbah 60:5, 14; Sanhedrin 95a)

traditions.text: Lists Abraham's servant with Saul and Jephthah as three men who asked improperly. His sign at the well could have been met by a lame or blind girl, and he had bound himself to take her for Isaac. God answered him better than he asked, the Talmud says, and sent Rebekah.

Reads Isaac's going out “to meditate in the field at the eventide” (v. 63) as prayer, since the same Hebrew word is used of pouring out a complaint before the LORD in Psalm 102:1. On this basis it credits Isaac with instituting the afternoon prayer, as Abraham did the morning prayer and Jacob the evening prayer.

Fills in why Isaac brings Rebekah into his mother's tent. While Sarah lived, a cloud hung over the tent, its doors stood open to guests, a blessing rested on her dough, and a lamp burned from one Sabbath eve to the next; all four stopped at her death and returned when Rebekah came. Only then, seeing she was like his mother, did Isaac take her in.

Works out the dates: Isaac marries at 40, in Abraham's 140th year, three years after Sarah's death. He then reads the oath with the servant's hand under Abraham's thigh as a sign that the God of heaven and earth would come in the flesh descended from that thigh. For Augustine the custom of the oath becomes a small prophecy of Christ.
